overview: A 6-axis force/torque (F/T) sensor is a compact metal puck bolted between a robot arm's wrist and its end effector, measuring the full wrench applied at that interface: three forces (Fx, Fy, Fz) and three torques (Mx, My, Mz) simultaneously, not just a single push/pull number. Internally it's a machined elastic structure (often a Stewart-platform-like spoke arrangement) instrumented with multiple strain-gauge bridges whose combined readings are resolved through a calibration matrix into the six independent components. This is what lets a robot 'feel' contact during force-controlled assembly, polishing, or human collaboration instead of blindly following a position trajectory. Unlike a single load cell, it can distinguish a straight push from an off-axis nudge or a twisting moment, which is exactly the information a compliant-motion controller needs.
simpleSummary: A sensor puck bolted onto a robot's wrist that lets it feel exactly how hard, and in which direction and twist, something is pushing back.

specifications.resolution: ~0.05 N force, ~0.0015 N·m torque (16-bit ADC per strain channel)
specifications.outputInterface: RS-485, Modbus RTU, half-duplex differential pair
specifications.sampleRate: up to 1 kHz over RS-485 (internal strain ADCs sample faster, ~7.8 kHz per axis, and are digitally filtered)
specifications.singleAxisOverload: typically 2-3x rated capacity before permanent zero-offset shift or damage
specifications.mountingInterface: circular bolt-circle flanges on both faces, ISO 9409-1 compatible on many robot-mount models

pinMap.name: V+
pinMap.function: Positive supply input for the sensor's strain-gauge excitation, amplifiers, and RS-485 transceiver.
pinMap.gotcha: Running this off the same unfiltered 24V rail as a motor driver or contactor coil injects switching noise straight into the strain-gauge front end; give it its own filtered/regulated feed or expect noisy low-order counts even though the sensor itself is fine.

pinMap.name: V-
pinMap.function: Power return / supply ground, referenced to V+.
pinMap.gotcha: This is the power return, not the cable shield — tying them together at the sensor end is a common way to create a ground loop that shows up as low-level torque-channel noise.

pinMap.name: RS485_A
pinMap.function: Non-inverting differential data line for the Modbus RTU output stream carrying all six wrench channels.
pinMap.gotcha: Needs a 120 ohm termination resistor at each physical end of the bus, not at every sensor — over-terminating a short bench run usually still works, but under-terminating a longer run causes intermittent frame corruption that looks like a flaky sensor.

pinMap.name: RS485_B
pinMap.function: Inverting differential data line, paired with RS485_A.
pinMap.gotcha: Swapping A/B relative to the rest of the bus doesn't damage anything but reliably produces zero valid frames — if a freshly wired sensor reads nothing on an otherwise healthy bus, try swapping this pair first.

pinMap.name: SYNC
pinMap.function: Optional external trigger input (TTL) used to time-align sampling across multiple F/T sensors or with a motion controller's servo cycle.
pinMap.gotcha: Leaving this floating on some firmware revisions can free-run or spuriously trigger sampling; if you're not using multi-sensor sync, tie it to a known level rather than leaving it unconnected.

pinMap.name: SHIELD
pinMap.function: Cable shield / drain connection to the connector housing, intended to be grounded to earth at one point in the system.
pinMap.gotcha: Grounding the shield at both the sensor end and the controller end creates a ground loop through the chassis; the standard practice is single-point grounding at the controller cabinet only.

useCases.title: Force-controlled peg-in-hole assembly
useCases.scenario: Monitor Fz and the small Mx/My torques while inserting a part, backing off and re-approaching on a search spiral when resistance spikes instead of grinding through a misalignment.

useCases.title: Human-robot collaborative contact safety
useCases.scenario: Continuously watch the wrench magnitude at the tool flange and trigger a protective stop or compliant retreat if contact force exceeds a safety-rated threshold, per collaborative robot safety standards.

useCases.title: Robotic deburring / surface finishing
useCases.scenario: Hold a constant normal force (Fz) against a curved workpiece surface while the tool path moves tangentially, compensating automatically for part-to-part shape variation.

useCases.title: Bin-picking grasp verification
useCases.scenario: After closing the gripper, check Fz and torque signatures to confirm a real part is held (and not slipping) before committing to the transport move, rather than trusting gripper position alone.

useCases.title: Multi-sensor synchronized force logging
useCases.scenario: Use the SYNC input across several F/T sensors on a test rig so every sensor's sample corresponds to the exact same instant, needed for research-grade multi-axis load characterization.

oftenConfusedWith: Load cell + HX711 amplifier (measures one axis of force only; this sensor resolves a full 6-component wrench — 3 forces and 3 torques — simultaneously)
In-line rotary torque sensor (measures a single torque about one shaft axis for drivetrain testing, not a spatial force/torque wrench at a tool interface)
oftenUpgradedTo: EtherCAT or fieldbus-output F/T sensors with higher sample rates for tight real-time force-control loops

beginnerMistakes: Exceeding a single axis's overload rating during a fast collision or a mistuned force-control loop — this can permanently shift the calibration zero-offset even when the sensor still 'works' and shows no visible damage.
Skipping the RS-485 termination resistors, which only becomes obvious as corrupted frames under EMI or on longer cable runs, not on a short bench test.
Not taring/zeroing the sensor after mounting the end effector — the tool's own weight and any asymmetric mass bias every reading until it's zeroed in that orientation.
Grounding the cable shield at both ends instead of one, introducing a ground loop that shows up as low-level noise on the torque channels specifically.
Treating the sensor as a perfectly rigid structural link in fast motions — it has real mechanical compliance, and ignoring that can excite resonance in a tightly tuned force-control loop.
